claims.text: The target sample is concentrated, bulk crystalline HfNbTaTiZr with less than 1 wt.% oxygen and no other defects.
The proposed framework independently computes lattice and electronic heat transport.
Lattice transport will be calculated using anharmonic phonon Boltzmann transport with explicit disorder-induced scattering.
Electronic transport will be calculated using a DFT-based Kubo–Greenwood method.
The dual-channel framework will reduce predictive error by approximately 25–50% relative to Debye-temperature-based models.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable below 200 K.
The framework will reliably predict total thermal conductivity of low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Atomic-scale compositional disorder produces variations in local interatomic environments in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Variations in interatomic force constants and anharmonic effects influence phonon lifetimes in HfNbTaTiZr.
Detailed electronic band-structure effects influence electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Separating lattice and electronic transport avoids oversimplifications inherent in single-parameter models.
Explicit treatment of phonon scattering, anharmonicity, and electronic structure will reduce overall predictive error.
Existing baseline methods conflate lattice and electronic contributions through averaged parameters such as a single Debye temperature.
The proposed approach is applicable only to well-controlled, defect-free or low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr samples.
Significant oxygen contamination or other unmodeled defects can introduce additional scattering and diminish predictive accuracy.
Precise experimental separation of lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions below 200 K is challenging.
Thermal diffusivity and Seebeck measurements can be used together to disentangle lattice and electronic heat transport at low temperature.
Inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering can provide phonon-lifetime measurements for assessing the lattice contribution.
Failure to reduce predictive error by at least 25% relative to a Debye-temperature baseline falsifies the hypothesis.
A deviation greater than ±25% between predicted and independently measured low-temperature lattice or electronic contributions falsifies the hypothesis.
